newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Paribas to sell Credit du Nord.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Paribas to sell Credit du Nord.

text.p: French financial holding company Paribas will start talks on a quick sale of its retail banking unit Credit du Nord to Societe Generale for 2.2 billion francs ($415 million), the two companies announced on Thursday.

The move was well viewed by analysts, who said it allowed Paribas to divest itself of retail banking and concentrate on its core businesses and helped Societe Generale meet a goal of boosting its domestic retail banking presence.

The two companies said in a joint statement the transaction would take place in two stages. "During the first phase, Societe Generale would take a controlling interest in Credit du Nord and would make a commitment to acquire the remainder of the company's equity within the next three years," they said.
Paribas has been trying since 1995 to get rid of its retail banking business to concentrate on international investment and merchant banking, and specialised financial services.
The joint statement said that for Societe Generale, the deal "offers a strategic fit with its objective of expanding retail banking operations in France."
Credit du Nord will benefit from the support of a major retail bank to accelerate its development and improve profitability, it said.
Banking analysts said the move was very good for Paribas, which said it would make a 600 million franc capital gain from the sale, but perhaps a less obvious positive for the acquirer.
And while some said the move could be seen as the latest in a budding and much-needed consolidation of France's financial sector, not all agreed.
"What's changed? They've (Credit du Nord) changed owners but that's about it," said Sheila Garrard, banking analyst at Lehman Brothers.
She noted that the statement said Societe Generale and Credit du Nord would remain "separate entities" and that Credit du Nord would "maintain its distinctive identity, its franchise and its brands".
"Some people see this as a consolidation but I'm not sure I do," Garrard said.
Analysts said they agreed that the purchase fitted Societe Generale's strategy of trying to increase its retail power in France, but said it might have some short-term negative effects.
"For Societe Generale, this will allow it to match Banque Nationale de Paris in size," said Jean-Baptiste Bellon, analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Financially, the impact will be very slightly dilutive for results, but it's more difficult to say in terms of shareholders' capital," Bellon said.
Bellon said Credit du Nord held about one percent of France's retail banking market.
The stock market cheered the deal, sending shares in Paribas and Societe General 3.61 percent and 0.93 percent higher, respectively.

The initial acquisition by Societe Generale of a controlling share in Credit du Nord, giving it the majority of voting rights, would involve a 2.5 billion franc capital increase, reserved to Societe Generale, accompanied by a share purchase.

The capital rise would bring Credit du Nord's tier one capital ratio in line with Societe Generale's standards. For Paribas, the sale price of its Credit du Nord shares reflected its revised net asset value of 1.6 billion francs on Paribas' books.
